sections.text: CKE Throughput Unit

sections.heading: The 1 PB/s North-Star Unit
sections.text: C-Kernel-Engine cares about a practical systems question: how fast can the cumulative compute system cycle active model data to produce tokens? FLOPS and TOPS are useful hardware numbers, but they do not directly answer

sections.heading: The Unit
sections.text: CKU = active_bytes_per_token / seconds_per_token CKU means C-Kernel throughput unit . The unit is not just DRAM bandwidth from one socket and it is not just matrix FLOPS. It is an end-to-end systems rate: how many bytes

sections.heading: Not Just Weights
sections.text: A common shortcut is to say, "a 1 TB model at 1 ms/token needs 1 PB/s." That is a useful intuition, but it is not the full CKU definition. CKU is not only parameter bytes divided by token time. It is the active byte path

sections.heading: Why 1 PB/s?
sections.text: A very large modern model can easily imply hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes of active weight and state movement across the token path, especially before accounting for prefill, KV cache, MoE routing, recurrent state, o

sections.heading: What Counts as Active Bytes?
sections.text: Active bytes are the bytes that matter for the current token path. They are not the total size of every file on disk and they are not necessarily the total parameter count of the model. For a dense model, the active path

sections.heading: Lifecycle Envelope and Concurrency
sections.text: CKU is first a single-stream lifecycle unit . It asks what the runtime must cycle for one model instance serving one token path at the model's intended operating envelope. If a model advertises a 1 million token context

sections.heading: Node Roofline Math
sections.text: CKU is not only a memory-bandwidth number and it is not only a FLOPS number. A CPU node can only contribute the useful part of the slowest roof: memory bandwidth, compute throughput, or network movement when the run is d

sections.heading: Refinement: Not All Bytes Cross All Roofs

sections.text: Distributed CKE needs the unit to separate what the hardware could do from what the system does do. Potential CKU sums independently measured node capability; realized CKU is the useful path advanced per wall-clock secon

sections.heading: One public CKU; per-region rates are the planner's pricing

sections.heading: Attention Mechanisms
sections.text: Attention is the core of transformers: it lets each token "look at" all other tokens and decide what's relevant.

sections.heading: Attention Math
sections.text: 1. Project input to Q, K, V: Q = input @ W_q # What am I looking for? K = input @ W_k # What do I contain? V = input @ W_v # What do I offer? 2. Compute attention scores: scores = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k) # How relevant is ea

sections.heading: Why Scale by sqrt(d_k)?
sections.text: Without scaling, dot products grow with dimension size, pushing softmax into saturation (all attention on one token). Scaling keeps gradients healthy. d_k = 64: scale = 1/8 = 0.125 d_k = 128: scale = 1/11.3 ≈ 0.088

sections.heading: Flash Attention
sections.text: Flash Attention is an algorithmic optimization that computes exact attention without materializing the full N×N attention matrix. It's about memory efficiency, not approximation.

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.text: Standard attention materializes the full score matrix: scores = Q @ K.T # [N, N] matrix! N = 2048: 16 MB N = 8192: 256 MB N = 32768: 4 GB N = 131072: 64 GB # Won't fit in GPU! Memory is O(N²), which limits context length

sections.heading: Flash Attention Solution
sections.text: Process in tiles , never storing full N×N matrix: Load Q tile to fast SRAM Stream K, V tiles through Compute partial softmax with online algorithm Accumulate output incrementally Memory: O(N) instead of O(N²) Speed: 2-4x

sections.text: Sliding-window attention limits each query to the most recent W tokens. It is exact within the window, keeps compute linear in sequence length, and provides predictable latency for long contexts.

sections.heading: Context
sections.text: In IR v3, model architecture was embedded in build_layer_layout() . Adding new models required modifying core codegen.

sections.heading: Decision
sections.text: Templates are the canonical definition of model architectures. The IR is a compiled artifact derived from templates + config.json. # templates/qwen2.yaml name: qwen2 config_mapping: hidden_size: embed_dim num_attention_h

sections.heading: Context
sections.text: Transformer inference has fundamentally different execution patterns: Prefill : Process entire prompt (T tokens, large buffers) Decode : Generate one token (T=1, KV cache reused) Backward : Compute gradients for training

sections.heading: Decision
sections.text: Allocate separate activation buffers for each execution mode. Weights are shared, working memory is mode-specific. ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ MEMORY LAYOUT │ ├──────────────────────

sections.text: All arrays are flat row-major FP32 buffers. The head dimension is outermost for cache-friendly per-head iteration.

sections.heading: Reference (
sections.text: _ref ) Pure scalar C — no intrinsics Triple-nested loops: head → row → col Used for parity testing against llama.cpp Bit-exact reference for correctness

sections.heading: AVX (
sections.text: _avx ) 256-bit SIMD — 8 floats per instruction Pre-normalizes q̂ / k̂ before the state sweep Single row walk per state-matrix pass Scalar tail loop for non-multiple-of-8 dims

sections.heading: AVX2 + FMA (
sections.text: _avx2 ) Same 256-bit width, adds FMA: a×b+c in 1 cycle 2-row unroll : processes rows in pairs to halve loop overhead Uses _mm256_fmadd_ps where available Falls back to mul+add without FMA flag

sections.heading: AVX-512 (
sections.text: _avx512 ) 512-bit SIMD — 16 floats per instruction Native FMA via _mm512_fmadd_ps Uses _mm512_reduce_add_ps for hsum Largest vector width = fewest iterations

sections.heading: CK-Engine Kernel Rules
sections.text: Like all CK kernels, the DeltaNet implementation follows strict rules:

sections.heading: 🚫 No malloc / free
sections.text: Memory comes via bump allocator. All pointers are passed in. Stack arrays ( CK_DELTANET_MAX_STACK_DIM = 4096 ) are used for temporaries.

sections.heading: 🚫 No OpenMP
sections.text: Parallelization happens at the orchestrator/codegen layer. Kernels are single-threaded, deterministic units.

sections.heading: ✅ Pure computation
sections.text: No side effects, no global state. Given the same inputs, produces identical outputs. Essential for parity testing.

sections.heading: ✅ Defined API contract
sections.text: Every kernel declares: inputs, outputs, workspace requirements, and memory layouts. The dispatcher selects ISA at compile time.

sections.heading: DeltaNet vs SSM (Mamba): Two Paths Beyond Attention

sections.heading: GEMM vs GEMV in Production LLM Serving
sections.text: In transformer inference, most expensive linear layers reduce to either GEMM or GEMV. The distinction matters because a kernel that is good for one can be poor for the other.

sections.heading: GEMV: decode latency
sections.text: GEMV is matrix-vector multiplication: one new token is multiplied by a weight matrix. This is the common decode path after the prompt is already in the KV cache. // Decode, one token output[1, N] = activation[1, K] x wei

sections.heading: GEMM: prefill throughput
sections.text: GEMM is matrix-matrix multiplication: many prompt tokens are processed together. This is the prefill path and the dominant cost for long prompts. // Prefill, M prompt tokens output[M, N] = activations[M, K] x weight[N, K

sections.heading: Why simple correctness kernels are not production kernels
sections.text: A reference kernel proves the math. A production kernel has to prove the data movement. The same equation can run 3x slower if it repeatedly reloads cache lines, transposes buffers between operators, dispatches too many

sections.heading: 1. Shape first
sections.text: Measure real model shapes, not synthetic square matrices only. Qwen2, Qwen3, Gemma, Nanbeige, and vision models stress different M/N/K regimes.

sections.heading: 2. Layout before instruction count
sections.text: If the weight layout forces scattered loads or repeated unpacking, more SIMD instructions will not fix the bottleneck. Repacking and interleaving often matter more than another arithmetic trick.

sections.heading: 3. Cache reuse
sections.text: Fast GEMM keeps reused A/B tiles close to the core. Fast GEMV streams weights predictably and avoids extra copies around activations, logits, and head-major attention output.

sections.heading: 4. Threading policy
sections.text: More threads are not automatically better. Small GEMV and tiny-M prefill can regress when threadpool overhead and memory contention exceed useful work.

sections.heading: 5. Quantization path
sections.text: Quantized inference is usually Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K weights times Q8_K or Q8_0 activations. Test the actual mixed-format kernel, not only dequantize-to-FP32 fallback.

sections.heading: 6. Parity gates
sections.text: Keep exact/reference kernels available. Enable optimized kernels by dispatch only after they pass llama.cpp/PyTorch parity for the relevant format and shape.

sections.heading: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants
sections.text: Our GEMM implementation draws from decades of high-performance computing research and industry-leading libraries:

sections.heading: The 8x8 Microkernel Architecture
sections.text: The heart of our GEMM is an 8x8 microkernel that keeps all 64 accumulator values in AVX registers throughout the entire K-loop. This is the same strategy used by oneDNN and BLIS.

sections.heading: Matrix Packing for Cache Efficiency
sections.text: For large matrices, we pack A and B into contiguous memory layouts that maximize cache line utilization. This is the key technique that allowed us to beat MKL.

sections.heading: Three-Level Cache Blocking
sections.text: We tile the computation to fit each level of the memory hierarchy, minimizing data movement between DRAM and CPU.

sections.heading: Our Optimization Journey

sections.text: GGUF to Bump Allocator This document explains how C-Kernel-Engine handles quantized weights from GGUF files (llama.cpp format) and converts them to our bump allocator layout for efficient inference and training. 📖 Prereq

sections.heading: Why Quantization Matters
sections.text: 4x Memory Reduction Q4_K uses ~4.5 bits/weight vs 32 bits for FP32 2x Bandwidth Savings Less data to move from DRAM = faster inference <1% Quality Loss Q4_K_M preserves model quality remarkably well

sections.heading: GGUF File Format Overview
sections.text: GGUF (GGML Universal Format) is llama.cpp's binary format for storing quantized models. Understanding it is essential for our conversion pipeline.

sections.heading: Q4_K Block Structure
sections.text: Q4_K is a "K-quant" format with nested scales. Each super-block contains 256 weights organized into 8 sub-blocks of 32 weights each. This two-level scaling provides better accuracy than simple 4-bit quantization.

sections.heading: Scale Unpacking (The Tricky Part)
sections.text: The 12-byte scales array packs 8 scales and 8 mins in 6-bit format. Unpacking requires careful bit manipulation:

sections.heading: 6-bit Packed Layout
sections.text: // scales[12] = 96 bits = 16 x 6-bit values // First 8 values: scales (sc[0..7]) // Last 8 values: mins (m[0..7]) // Unpacking sc[0..7] from bytes 0-5: sc[0] = scales[0] & 0x3F; // bits 0-5 of byte 0 sc[1] = (scales[0] >

sections.heading: Bump File Header Format
sections.text: The bump allocator uses a 128-byte header that contains all model configuration needed at runtime: // Bump Header Structure (128 bytes total) // ======================================== Offset Size Field Description ----

sections.heading: Cache Line Alignment
sections.text: Modern CPUs fetch data in 64-byte cache lines. Misaligned access causes: Two cache line fetches instead of one Cache line splitting penalties Reduced SIMD throughput

sections.heading: AVX-512 Requirements
sections.text: AVX-512 processes 16 floats (64 bytes) per instruction: Aligned loads: _mm512_load_ps (fast) Unaligned loads: _mm512_loadu_ps (slower) Padding zeros don't affect results

sections.heading: Per-Layer Weight Layout
sections.text: Each transformer layer's weights are stored contiguously in the bump file:

sections.heading: Dequantization Kernels
sections.text: At inference time, we dequantize weights on-the-fly during GEMM operations. This trades compute for memory bandwidth - a good trade on modern CPUs where memory is the bottleneck.

sections.text: GGUF to Bump: Step-by-Step Conversion This document walks through every step of converting a GGUF file to C-Kernel-Engine's bump allocator format. We'll trace through the actual bytes, show the parsing logic, and explain

sections.heading: Step 1: Read and Validate Magic
sections.text: Every GGUF file starts with the 4-byte magic string "GGUF". This identifies the file format and catches truncated or corrupted files early.

sections.heading: Code: Magic Validation
sections.text: magic = f.read(4) if magic != b"GGUF": raise GGUFError(f"Invalid magic {magic!r} (expected b'GGUF')")

sections.heading: Step 2: Parse GGUF Header
sections.text: After the magic, we read the version and counts. GGUF v2+ uses 64-bit counts (v1 used 32-bit).

sections.heading: Code: Header Parsing
sections.text: version = r.u32() # Read 4-byte unsigned int if version >= 2: n_tensors = r.u64() # 8-byte count n_kv = r.u64() else: n_tensors = r.u32() # v1: 4-byte count n_kv = r.u32() # Sanity check (catches corrupt headers) if n_te

sections.heading: Step 3: Read Metadata Key-Value Pairs
sections.text: GGUF metadata contains model configuration. We only parse the keys we need and skip the rest for performance (especially important for large tokenizer arrays).

sections.heading: Keys We Extract
sections.text: GGUF Key Type Maps To Example general.architecture string model_type "llama" llama.block_count u32 num_layers 36 llama.embedding_length u32 hidden_size 3584 llama.feed_forward_length u32 intermediate_size 18944 llama.att

sections.heading: Code: Selective Metadata Parsing
sections.text: wanted_meta = { "general.architecture", "llama.block_count", "llama.embedding_length", # ... other keys we need } meta = {} for _ in range(n_kv): key = r.key_str() # Read key length + key bytes vtype = r.u32() # Read val

sections.heading: Step 4: Read Tensor Info (Headers Only)
sections.text: For each tensor, we read its name, dimensions, type, and offset within the data section. The actual tensor data comes later - this is just the index.

sections.heading: Code: Building Tensor Index
sections.text: @dataclass class TensorInfo: name: str dims: Tuple[int, ...] # GGML order: ne0, ne1, ... ggml_type: int offset: int # Relative to data section start tensors: Dict[str, TensorInfo] = {} for _ in range(n_tensors): name = r

sections.heading: Step 5: Calculate Data Section Start (Alignment)
sections.text: GGUF aligns the data section to a boundary (typically 32 bytes). This ensures tensor data is properly aligned for SIMD operations.

sections.heading: Code: Calculate and Seek to Data
sections.text: alignment = meta.get("general.alignment", 32) # Default 32 bytes # Current position after reading all tensor info current_pos = r.tell() # Align to boundary data_start = ((current_pos + alignment - 1) // alignment) * ali

sections.heading: Step 6: Build Dtype Table
sections.text: The bump format stores a per-tensor dtype table so the runtime knows which dequantization kernel to use. Each tensor gets a 1-byte type code.

sections.heading: Code: Build Dtype Table
sections.text: # Start with token embedding dtype token_dtype = ck_dtype_from_ggml_type(tok.ggml_type) dtype_table = [token_dtype, CK_DT_FP32] # tok_emb, pos_emb # Per-layer dtypes (14 entries per layer) for layer in range(num_layers):

sections.heading: Step 7: Write Bump Header
sections.text: The bump header is 128 bytes containing everything the runtime needs to interpret the weight data. We write a placeholder first, then fill it in after computing the SHA-256 checksum.

sections.heading: Step 8: Stream Tensor Data
sections.text: This is where the actual conversion happens. We read tensors from GGUF and write them to bump in a specific order. Importantly, we don't dequantize - we copy the quantized blocks directly.

sections.heading: 1. Norm Vectors: FP16/BF16 → FP32
sections.text: GGUF stores RMSNorm gammas as FP16 or BF16. We convert to FP32 for the kernel: def read_vector_f32(f, info): raw = f.read(row_bytes) if info.ggml_type == GGML_TYPE_F16: return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float16).astype(np.flo

sections.heading: 2. Q/K/V: Head-Packed Layout
sections.text: GGUF stores Q/K/V as flat [in_dim × out_dim]. We repack per-head for aligned access: # For each head, copy head_dim rows # Then pad to aligned_head_dim if needed for head in range(num_heads): for row in range(head_dim):

sections.heading: 3. Q4_K Blocks: Direct Copy (No Dequant!)
sections.text: The key optimization: we copy quantized blocks byte-for-byte. Dequantization happens at inference time in the GEMM kernel. def copy_bytes_stream(f_in, src_pos, nbytes, w_out, chunk=1MB): """Stream copy without loading en

sections.heading: Checksumming
sections.text: After writing all data, we compute a SHA-256 checksum over the payload (everything after the 128-byte header). This catches corruption during download or storage.

sections.heading: Code: Checksum with HashingWriter
sections.text: class HashingWriter: """Wraps file writes to compute running SHA-256""" def __init__(self, f): self._f = f self._h = hashlib.sha256() self.bytes_written = 0 def write(self, data): self._f.write(data) self._h.update(data)

sections.heading: Operator Start Here (Snapshot: February 11, 2026)
sections.text: If you revisit this page in six months, begin with the gate entrypoint first. It encodes the current v6.6 release contract better than any prose summary.

sections.heading: One Command First
sections.text: make v6.6-gate This runs kernel-map sync, tooling contracts, matrix smoke, parity matrix (runtime-optional), and long-decode stability in sequence.

sections.heading: Runtime Modes and Preconditions
sections.text: v6.6 operates in two practical modes: build-smoke mode and full-parity mode. Full parity requires llama parity runtime artifacts; without them, strict parity gates can report SKIP and fail under --require-all .

sections.heading: Minimal Preflight (No Parity Runtime)

sections.heading: Full Release Gate (Parity Required)
sections.text: make llamacpp-parity-build make v6.6-gate make v6.6-validate-parity-matrix-required Use this path before release claims that depend on strict CK vs llama parity confidence.

sections.heading: Why IR1 Exists
sections.text: IR1 is the validation and contract layer . It ensures the template ops are valid, mapped, and supported before we allocate memory or emit C. This is the earliest point to fail fast.

sections.text: IR v2 Format Specification IR v2 is a self-documenting JSON format that captures model architecture, buffer definitions, and computation graphs in a portable, machine-readable format.

sections.heading: Key Features
sections.text: Portable - Same IR works for different batch sizes Self-documenting - Contains notes explaining the format Extensible - Supports encoder, decoder, and encoder-decoder architectures

sections.heading: Dimension Mapping
sections.text: The IR uses symbolic dimension IDs that map to actual values from the model config: ID Name Source in config.json Example (Qwen2-0.5B) 0 tokens batch_size x seq_len (runtime) 131072 1 embed hidden_size 896 2 aligned_embe

sections.heading: How Dimensions Resolve
sections.text: shape[{dim:10}] → dimensions[10] → {name:"vocab", value:151936} → 151936 elements Example: token_emb shape = [vocab, aligned_embed] = [151936, 896]

sections.heading: config.json
sections.text: (from HuggingFace) Downloaded automatically. Provides model dimensions. { "hidden_size": 896, "vocab_size": 151936, "num_attention_heads": 14, "num_key_value_heads": 2, "intermediate_size": 4864, "num_hidden_layers": 24

sections.heading: global_buffers.json
sections.text: (legacy_kernel_maps/) Defines global buffers using symbolic dimension names. {"buffers": [ {"name": "token_emb", "scope": "global", "role": "weight", "shape": [{"dim":"vocab"}, {"dim":"aligned_embed"}]} ]}

sections.heading: decoder_layer_plan.json
sections.text: (legacy_kernel_maps/) Defines operations in each transformer layer. {"steps": [ {"kernel": "rmsnorm", "bind": {"input": "input", "gamma": "ln1_gamma"}}, {"kernel": "qkv_project", ...}, {"kernel": "attention", ...} ]} The

sections.heading: ir_v2.json
sections.text: (Output) Self-documenting IR with all dimensions resolved. { "version": 2, "notes": ["...format guide..."], "dimensions": [...], "buffers": [...], "nodes": [...] }

sections.heading: Generate IR v2
sections.text: # Fetch config from HuggingFace make fetch-v2 IR_V2_HF=Qwen/Qwen2-0.5B # Generate IR v2 make ir-v2 IR_V2_HF=Qwen/Qwen2-0.5B # Generate C runtime ./build/ck_ir_v2_demo --ir build/ir_v2.json --emit build/generated_v2.c

sections.heading: For GGUF Quantized Models
sections.text: # Use the GGUF-specific repo make ir-v2 IR_V2_HF=Qwen/Qwen2-0.5B-Instruct-GGUF \ IR_V2_WEIGHTS=qwen2-0_5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf

sections.heading: IR Lowering
sections.text: The high-level IR is portable but not executable. The lowering pass converts it to a mode-specific form with a concrete memory plan.

sections.heading: Prefill Mode
sections.text: Process full sequence (prompt). All tokens in parallel. ./build/ck_ir_v2_demo config.json \ --lower prefill

sections.heading: Decode Mode
sections.text: Generate one token at a time. Uses KV cache. ./build/ck_ir_v2_demo config.json \ --lower decode \ --lower-out build/decode.json

sections.heading: Backward Mode
sections.text: Training. Auto-builds backward graph. ./build/ck_ir_v2_demo config.json \ --lower backward

sections.heading: Memory Layout Philosophy
sections.text: C-Kernel-Engine uses a single contiguous memory allocation for the entire model. This design is critical for CPU performance.

sections.heading: Why One Allocation?
sections.text: CPU doesn't care if data is a weight or activation - it just needs sequential memory access Single base pointer + offsets = simpler memory management, no pointer chasing Hugepage alignment (1GB/2MB) enables NUMA-aware pl

sections.heading: NUMA / Sub-NUMA Optimization
sections.text: With 1GB hugepages, each page can be placed on a different DRAM bank: Page 0 (0-1GB) → DRAM Bank 0 (Layer 0-5) Page 1 (1-2GB) → DRAM Bank 1 (Layer 6-11) Page 2 (2-3GB) → DRAM Bank 2 (Layer 12-17) ... While Layer 0 comput

sections.heading: Offset-Based Access
sections.text: All tensors accessed via offsets from single base pointer: typedef struct { size_t ln1_gamma; // weight size_t ln1_output; // activation size_t wq, wk, wv; // weights size_t q, k, v; // activations ... } LayerOffsets; //

sections.heading: Why NOT Separate Arenas?
sections.text: Separating weights/activations/gradients into different allocations would mean: 3+ base pointers to track (or 6+ with sections) Multiple malloc/canary regions to manage Cache misses when jumping between arenas Harder to

sections.heading: Shape Resolution
sections.text: Each shape dimension is {dim, mult, div} : size = dimensions[dim].value * mult / div

sections.heading: Buffer Roles
sections.text: weight - Model params activation - Runtime tensors grad - Gradients

sections.heading: Buffer Scope
sections.text: global - Shared across layers layer - Per-layer tensors

sections.text: CK C-Kernel-Engine High-Performance ML Kernels 🚀 Iteration Philosophy: v1→v6 and Beyond Why rapid iteration, continuous learning, and bold architectural changes drive breakthrough performance in kernel optimization 💡 Cor

sections.heading: 1. Constraint-Driven vs Specification-Driven Development
sections.text: 🎯 Core Insight: While everyone talks about spec-driven development, kernel optimization is driven by constraints, not specifications. Constraints are discovered, not defined.

sections.heading: 📋 Specification-Driven
sections.text: Assumption: We can define requirements upfront Write detailed specifications Design architecture to match spec Implement according to design Test against requirements Problem: Specifications become obsolete as we learn

sections.heading: ⚡ Constraint-Driven
sections.text: Reality: Constraints emerge during development Identify current constraints Design around known constraints Prototype to discover new constraints Iterate as constraints evolve Advantage: Adapt to reality, not assumptions

sections.heading: 💻 Hardware
sections.text: AVX-512 availability Cache hierarchy sizes Memory bandwidth limits NUMA topology

sections.heading: ⚡ Performance
sections.text: Inference latency targets Throughput requirements Context length limits Batch size trade-offs

sections.heading: 🔗 Compatibility
sections.text: Model format support API stability Type system Platform support Each iteration reveals new constraints and invalidates old assumptions. The architecture evolves to honor these discovered constraints.

sections.heading: 2. Why Iteration Matters in Kernel Development
sections.text: Kernel optimization is fundamentally experimental. Unlike application development where requirements are stable, kernel performance depends on: Hardware evolution: New CPU instructions (AVX-512, VNNI, AMX), cache hierarc

sections.heading: ❌ The Perfectionist Trap
sections.text: Spend months designing the "perfect" v1 architecture Implement everything at once with complex abstractions Discover fundamental flaws only after full implementation Painful, expensive refactoring required

sections.heading: ✅ The Iterative Approach
sections.text: Ship v1 with core ideas quickly (weeks, not months) Learn from real-world performance gaps Refactor aggressively in v2 based on learnings Each version builds on proven foundations

sections.heading: v1: Proof of Concept
sections.text: Goal: Can we build custom kernels that beat BLAS? Key Learning: Baseline performance achievable, but architectural debt accumulated Kept: Core kernel structure, basic quantization support Discarded: Over-engineered abstr

sections.heading: v2: IR Revolution
sections.text: Goal: Portable, optimized code generation Key Learning: IR-based approach enables rapid experimentation with different optimizations Kept: IR concept, kernel building blocks Discarded: Hardcoded kernel paths, architectur

sections.heading: v3: Quantization Breakthrough
sections.text: Goal: Multi-format quantization (Q4, Q5, Q6, Q8) Key Learning: Type-specific kernels vastly outperform generic approaches Kept: Block-based quantization, format abstraction Discarded: FP32-only kernels, limited quantizat

sections.heading: v4: Memory Architecture
sections.text: Goal: Deterministic, safe memory management Key Learning: Memory safety doesn't sacrifice performance with proper design Kept: Bump allocator, safety guarantees Discarded: Manual memory management, undefined behavior

sections.heading: v5: Threading & Scheduling
sections.text: Goal: Efficient multi-threading for attention kernels Key Learning: Work partitioning strategy matters more than thread count Kept: Chunk-based scheduling, OpenMP integration Discarded: Poorly designed work stealing, rac

sections.heading: v6: Flash Attention & Beyond
sections.text: Goal: Memory-efficient attention with competitive performance Key Learning: ggml's custom CPU approach beats BLAS for attention - learning from competition Kept: All proven v5 foundations, IR system, quantization formats

sections.heading: 3. Case Study: IR v2 - When Iteration Requires Starting Over
sections.text: 🔄 IR v2 demonstrates bold iteration: Sometimes iteration means keeping the concept but discarding everything else. IR v2 completely redesigned the representation while preserving the core IR idea.

sections.heading: IR v1: The Original Approach
sections.text: What it was: Tight coupling between IR and generated code Hardcoded dimension layouts Fixed buffer arrangements Limited portability across models Difficult to optimize for different hardware

sections.heading: IR v2: The Redesigned Approach
sections.text: What it became: Symbolic, portable model representation Symbolic dimensions: {vocab, embed, head_dim} that resolve at compile-time Explicit buffer layouts: Clean separation of concerns Model-agnostic: Works with any tran

sections.heading: How IR v2 Embodies Iteration Philosophy
sections.text: 1. Kept the Foundation The fundamental idea of IR-based code generation was sound and worth preserving 2. Discarded the Implementation Everything else - data structures, APIs, layouts - was redesigned from scratch based

sections.heading: 4. The Art of Selective Preservation
sections.text: ⚠️ Critical Skill: Knowing what to keep vs. what to discard. Preserving proven foundations while removing blockers to progress.

sections.heading: Performance-Critical Code
sections.text: Hand-optimized SIMD kernels Proven quantization formats Efficient memory layouts Cache-friendly access patterns

sections.heading: Architectural Foundations
sections.text: IR-based code generation Type abstraction layers Safe memory management Test infrastructure

sections.heading: Over-Engineering
sections.text: Abstractions that add overhead without benefits Premature generalization Complex code paths for edge cases Architectural dogmatism

sections.heading: Proven Inefficiencies
sections.text: Sub-optimal algorithms (even if "elegant") Poor work partitioning strategies Unnecessary dependencies Legacy compatibility layers

sections.heading: 5. Fast Idea Testing: The v(next) Strategy
sections.text: Every new version follows a predictable pattern: Identify the bottleneck: What prevents better performance? Generate hypotheses: 3-5 potential solutions Prototype rapidly: Build minimal proof-of-concept in days, not week

sections.heading: Example: Flash Attention v6
sections.text: Problem: Our attention implementation slower than ggml on several workloads Hypothesis 1: Need custom CPU kernels (not BLAS) Hypothesis 2: Different memory tiling strategy Hypothesis 3: Work partitioning based on context

sections.heading: 6. Compounding Knowledge
sections.text: Each iteration compounds knowledge:

sections.heading: 📊 Performance Data
sections.text: Benchmarks from v1-v5 reveal patterns about what works and what doesn't across different hardware and workloads

sections.heading: 🛠️ Technical Debt
sections.text: What we discarded in each version becomes institutional knowledge about avoiding similar mistakes

sections.heading: 🎯 Focus Areas
sections.text: Each version narrows focus to the most impactful optimizations, avoiding scattered effort

sections.heading: 7. Why This Works: The Mathematics of Iteration
sections.text: Consider the velocity of learning: Approach Time to Breakthrough Learning Rate Risk Perfect v1 Architecture 6-12 months Slow (1x) High (single point of failure) Iterative (v1→v6) 6 months (6 iterations) Fast (6x faster l

sections.heading: 8.1 When to Iterate vs. When to Persist
🚦 Iterate When:
sections.text: Fundamental bottleneck in architecture Performance plateau persists across 2-3 attempts Competitors demonstrate superior approaches Hardware support changes (new instructions, etc.)

sections.heading: 💪 Persist When:
sections.text: Approach is sound but implementation needs tuning Edge cases uncovered but core is solid Performance gains are marginal but consistent Infrastructure improvements unlock future gains

sections.heading: 8.2 The 70% Rule
sections.text: Ship when you're 70% happy with the architecture. The remaining 30% will be discovered through real-world usage and become the foundation for v(next). Why 70%? It's the sweet spot where you've solved the fundamental prob

sections.heading: 9. Looking Forward: v7 and Beyond
sections.text: The v6 plan already incorporates lessons from v1-v5: From v1: Keep IR-based approach but simplify code generation From v2: Portable but optimize for common cases From v3: Type-specific kernels remain critical From v4: Me

sections.heading: What's Next After v6?
sections.text: Already identified potential v7 directions: Adaptive algorithms: Automatically select best kernel based on workload characteristics Hardware introspection: Detect CPU features at runtime, generate optimal code paths Dist

sections.heading: 10. The Culture of Iteration
sections.text: Technical decisions are only part of the equation. Cultural adoption of iteration is equally critical:

sections.heading: Embrace Experimentation
sections.text: Celebrate learnings, not just successes Document why approaches were discarded Make it easy to try radical ideas Reward risk-taking within bounds

sections.heading: Build for Change
sections.text: Modular architecture enables swapping components Comprehensive tests catch regressions early Automated benchmarking tracks performance Version control preserves knowledge

sections.text: Kernel Tuning Methodology C-Kernel-Engine performance work is not a benchmark stunt. The goal is to make a CPU node behave like a serious compute device: correct first, measurable at every layer, then pushed toward the r

sections.heading: North Star
sections.text: CK should make each CPU node run as close as practical to its hardware limits, then compose those nodes into larger CPU-native systems. The engine is written from the ground up in C so the team can inspect, replace, prof

sections.heading: Hard Rule
sections.text: Performance changes must keep the model path valid. First-token parity must not regress. Multi-token mismatch must not move earlier without explanation. Practical prompts must remain coherent, not just syntactically aliv

sections.heading: Measurement Lanes
sections.text: The work is split into lanes so we do not confuse different questions. A short chat prompt, a 4096-token prefill test, an Intel Advisor dot, and a VTune hotspot report are all useful, but they answer different things.

sections.heading: Practical E2E Lane
sections.text: Run real prompts through cks-v8-run with the correct chat template, tokenizer, context length, and decode budget. This lane answers: does the model still speak coherently, follow the prompt, and produce useful output?

sections.heading: Fixed-Token Throughput Lane
sections.text: Use controlled prompt and decode token counts, such as p512 , p1024 , p2048 , or p4096 . This lane answers: how fast is prefill or decode when the model actually receives that many tokens?

sections.heading: Operator Profile Lane
sections.text: Enable CK profile CSV/JSON and rank time by operator. This lane answers: is the wall time in Q4/Q6 prefill, Q8 projection, attention, SwiGLU, quantization, sampling, or runtime overhead?

sections.heading: Microkernel Lab
sections.text: Extract one kernel with the production dimensions and run it alone. This lane answers: can this exact kernel reach the expected instruction rate before we wire it back into the full transformer?

sections.heading: Advisor Roofline Lane
sections.text: Use Intel Advisor to place loops by arithmetic intensity and throughput. This lane answers: should the next patch move the kernel right by increasing reuse, or up by improving SIMD and instruction efficiency?

sections.heading: VTune Lane
sections.text: Use VTune hotspots, uarch exploration, memory access, and threading analysis. This lane answers: are we retiring useful work, stuck on ports, memory-bound, cache-latency-bound, or underusing physical cores?

sections.heading: Context Is Not Tokens

sections.text: Memory Safety Design Document This page describes our memory safety design philosophy and planned features. Sections marked Planned are not yet implemented.

sections.heading: Philosophy: Safety Through Simplicity
sections.text: Rather than relying on language-level safety (Rust) or runtime garbage collection, C-Kernel-Engine achieves memory safety through architectural simplicity :

sections.heading: Traditional C Problems
sections.text: malloc / free scattered everywhere Use-after-free vulnerabilities Double-free crashes Runtime size calculations (overflow risk) Manual pointer arithmetic Unknown buffer boundaries

sections.heading: Our Approach
sections.text: One mmap at start, one munmap at end No frees during execution → no use-after-free Nothing to double-free All sizes from config at codegen time Pre-computed offsets, no pointer math Every buffer size baked into generated

sections.heading: Memory Allocation Hierarchy
sections.text: Why Huge Pages? A 540MB model needs 138,240 TLB entries with 4KB pages, but only 270 entries with 2MB huge pages. Fewer TLB misses = faster memory access.

sections.heading: The Fallback Hierarchy
sections.text: void *ck_huge_alloc(size_t bytes) { size_t len = align_up_bytes(bytes, HUGE_PAGE_SIZE); // 2MB alignment // 1. Try explicit huge pages (best performance) void *p = mmap(NULL, len, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MA

sections.heading: Step 1: MAP_HUGETLB (Explicit Huge Pages)
sections.text: What it does: Requests 2MB pages directly from the kernel's hugepage pool. Requirements: # Reserve 1GB of huge pages (512 × 2MB) echo 512 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages # Or make permanent in /etc/sysctl.conf vm.nr

sections.heading: Step 2: aligned_alloc + madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)
sections.text: What it does: Allocates 2MB-aligned memory, then hints to kernel to use Transparent Huge Pages (THP). // Allocate with 2MB alignment void *q = aligned_alloc(2 * 1024 * 1024, len); // Tell kernel: "I'd like huge pages her

sections.heading: Step 3: Regular 4KB Pages (Implicit Fallback)
sections.text: If madvise hint is ignored, you get regular pages. Still works, just more TLB pressure.

sections.heading: Understanding THP and madvise
sections.text: THP = Transparent Huge Pages A Linux kernel feature that automatically promotes 4KB pages to 2MB pages. madvise() is how you tell the kernel which memory regions to promote.

sections.heading: THP Modes
sections.text: # Check current mode cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled # [always] madvise never Mode Behavior madvise needed? Recommendation always Kernel promotes ALL allocations No, automatic Can cause stalls madvise Onl

sections.heading: How THP Modes Affect Your Code
sections.text: // Your allocation: void *q = aligned_alloc(2MB, 100MB); madvise(q, 100MB, MADV_HUGEPAGE); // What happens next depends on THP mode: mode = "always" Kernel already trying to promote everything. Your madvise is redundant

sections.heading: Timeline: What Actually Happens
sections.text: Time 0ms: aligned_alloc(100MB) → Kernel allocates 25,600 × 4KB pages Time 0ms: madvise(ptr, 100MB, MADV_HUGEPAGE) → Kernel marks region: "promote this when possible" Time 1ms: Your code continues running... → Still using

sections.heading: Block Quantization
sections.text: Weights are grouped into blocks (32 or 256). Each block has a shared scale factor, reducing overhead while maintaining accuracy. Larger blocks = better compression, smaller blocks = better accuracy.

sections.heading: Symmetric vs Asymmetric
sections.text: Symmetric (Q4_0, Q5_0, Q8_0): Values centered at 0. Formula: weight = (q - center) x d Asymmetric (Q4_1, Q5_1): Adds min offset. Formula: weight = q x d + m

sections.heading: Q4_K dmin: SUBTRACT not ADD!
sections.text: Common Bug: Q4_K uses weight = q x (d x sc) - (dmin x mn) The minus sign is critical! dmin encodes a positive offset that gets subtracted to shift the range down. Using + instead of - produces wrong outputs.

sections.heading: K-Quant Nested Scales
sections.text: K-quant formats use 2-level scaling: a super-block FP16 scale multiplied by per-sub-block 6-bit or int8 scales. This gives fine-grained control with minimal overhead.

sections.heading: 5-bit and 6-bit Packing
sections.text: Q5 and Q6 formats split bits across multiple byte arrays. Q5: 4 low bits in qs , 1 high bit in qh . Q6: 4 low bits in ql , 2 high bits in qh .

sections.heading: Q8_K: FP32 Scale + bsums
sections.text: Q8_K uses FP32 scale (not FP16!) for higher precision. The bsums field contains precomputed sums of 16 consecutive int8s for VNNI/AVX-512 dot product optimization.

sections.heading: Why Quantize?
sections.text: Large language models are memory-bound, not compute-bound. A 7B parameter model in FP32 requires 28 GB of memory just for weights. Quantization dramatically reduces this.

sections.heading: FP32 (32-bit)
sections.text: 28 GB for 7B params Full precision, no loss

sections.heading: INT8 (8-bit)
sections.text: 7 GB for 7B params 4x reduction, ~0.1% loss

sections.heading: INT4 (4-bit)
sections.text: 3.5 GB for 7B params 8x reduction, ~0.5% loss

sections.heading: Memory Bandwidth is the Bottleneck
sections.text: Modern CPUs can do billions of FLOPs/second, but memory bandwidth is limited: Hardware Compute Memory BW Arithmetic Intensity Needed Intel Xeon Gold 6542Y ~4 TFLOPS (FP32) ~300 GB/s 13 FLOPS/byte NVIDIA A100 19.5 TFLOPS

sections.heading: Floating Point Primer
sections.text: Before diving into quantization, let's understand what we're compressing.

sections.heading: FP32 Format (32 bits)
sections.text: S 1 bit Exponent 8 bits Mantissa (Fraction) 23 bits Value = (-1)^S x 2^(E-127) x 1.Mantissa Example: 0.15625 Sign: 0 (positive) Exponent: 01111100 (124 - 127 = -3) Mantissa: 01000000000000000000000 (1.25) = 1 x 2^(-3) x

sections.heading: BF16 Format (16 bits)
sections.text: S 1 bit Exponent 8 bits Mantissa 7 bits Same exponent range as FP32 , but reduced precision (7 bits = ~2 decimal digits). Relative error: ~7.8e-3 (~0.78%). This is why our BF16 kernel tests use 1e-2 tolerance.

sections.heading: Basic Quantization Math
sections.text: Quantization maps continuous floating-point values to discrete integers.

sections.heading: Symmetric Quantization
sections.text: # Quantize: FP32 -> INT scale = max(abs(weights)) / (2^(bits-1) - 1) quantized = round(weights / scale) # Dequantize: INT -> FP32 dequantized = quantized * scale Example (INT8, range [-127, 127]): weights = [-0.5, 0.2, 1

sections.heading: Asymmetric Quantization
sections.text: # Also stores zero-point for non-symmetric distributions scale = (max - min) / (2^bits - 1) zero_point = round(-min / scale) quantized = round(weights / scale) + zero_point # Useful when weights are not centered around z

sections.heading: The Problem with Single Scales
sections.text: Consider a weight matrix with values ranging from -2.0 to +2.0, where some small but important values exist around 0.01:

sections.heading: Grouping: The Solution
sections.text: Instead of one scale for the entire matrix, use per-group scales . Each group gets its own scale, tailored to its local range.

sections.heading: Group 1: Large Values
sections.text: Values: [-2.0, 1.5, 0.8, -1.2] Local max: 2.0 Scale: 2.0 / 7 = 0.286 Each value uses full INT4 range relative to THIS group's scale.

sections.heading: Group 2: Small Values
sections.text: Values: [0.01, -0.005, 0.008, 0.003] Local max: 0.01 Scale: 0.01 / 7 = 0.00143 Now small values use full range! 0.01 -> 7, -0.005 -> -4, etc.

sections.heading: Why Group Size Matters
sections.text: Group Size Scale Overhead Precision Use Case 32 1 FP16 per 32 weights Best Q4_0, Q8_0 (common) 64 1 FP16 per 64 weights Good Some custom formats 128 1 FP16 per 128 weights Medium Aggressive compression 256 Nested scales

sections.text: Understanding cache behavior is critical for quantized kernel performance.

sections.heading: Cache Line Basics
sections.text: Cache line size: 64 bytes (typical x86) Q4_0 block: 18 bytes -> ~3.5 blocks per cache line Q4_K block: 144 bytes -> 2.25 cache lines per block Key insight: Scale and weights should be in SAME cache line when possible for

sections.heading: Good: Q4_0 Access

sections.text: Scaling Philosophy

sections.heading: The Bet Behind This Project
sections.text: The bet here is simple: AI will not stay locked inside premium proprietary boxes forever. C-Kernel-Engine takes a different path: Linux-only, CPU-only, server-grade hardware, open software, and standard data-center parts

sections.heading: 🧭 Engineering Compass — What This Page Is Really For
sections.text: This page is the reminder to stay focused on the real thesis: make CPU-only Linux systems useful for modern AI by improving the software until commodity server hardware becomes practical. The scaling story is a direction

sections.heading: The Two First Principles
sections.text: CPU Horizontal Scaling Can Stay Simpler Adding CPU servers still requires sharding, scheduling, networking, and NUMA discipline. But it avoids vendor-specific programming models, specialized accelerator fabrics, and the

sections.heading: The Computation Is Not Exotic
sections.text: AI training and inference reduce to five operations: matrix multiply, attention, softmax, layer normalization, and backpropagation. These are linear algebra and calculus — mathematics developed in the 17th through 19th c

sections.heading: The Google Precedent: Treat the Fleet as the Computer
sections.text: Google's early advantage was not a processor that was individually faster than every high-end server CPU. It combined commodity-class machines with fault-tolerant software and optimized the fleet for throughput, price-pe

sections.heading: The GPU Memory Trap
sections.text: Yes, you CAN fit a 70B model on GPUs using tensor/pipeline parallelism. That's not the point. The point is: you're now FORCED to buy 8+ GPUs in a cluster. And GPUs are: Proprietary — locked to NVIDIA (CUDA), no open ecos

sections.text: GPU Path: Model doesn't fit in 80GB → Buy 8 GPUs → $320K for GPUs alone Need NVLink for fast communication → Another $50K+ Need DGX chassis → Another $80K+ Total: $450K+ just to START CPU Path: Model fits in 4TB RAM → Bu

sections.heading: Why CPU-Only?
sections.text: GPUs dominate when you can keep them highly utilized. Large batches, dense GEMMs, and well-packed workloads that fit comfortably in VRAM let GPUs exercise their theoretical FLOPS advantage. C-Kernel-Engine isn't anti-GPU

sections.heading: Advantages
sections.text: No vendor lock-in - Works on any x86/ARM CPU Commodity hardware - Standard servers, not $40K GPUs Larger memory - 2TB RAM per node, no 80GB VRAM limit Better debugging - GDB, Valgrind, perf all work Simpler deployment -

sections.heading: The Trade-off
sections.text: GPUs have higher peak FLOPS But: memory bandwidth often bottlenecks anyway But: PCIe transfer overhead for large models But: multi-GPU coordination is complex But: CPU memory is 10-100x larger and cheaper For inference:

sections.heading: The Fundamental Math: 0 × ∞ = 0
sections.text: The Memory Constraint It doesn't matter how fast your compute is if your model won't fit in memory. Being 10x faster at computing doesn't help if you're limited by 0 × ∞ = 0.

sections.heading: CPU: Memory Wins
sections.text: Dual-socket server: 4-6TB DDR5 Can train: 1TB model in BF16 Math: 4-6TB × dual socket = non-zero, model loads Result: Actually trains the model

sections.heading: GPU: Compute Fast, Memory Fails
sections.text: Single GPU VRAM: tops out well below what large models need Each GPU generation: more HBM — at exponentially higher price per unit The constraint: 1TB model ÷ per-GPU VRAM = many GPUs, minimum, just for weights Math: 0 u

sections.heading: GPUs Require Clusters
sections.text: Here's the fundamental problem: no single GPU can handle large models. You need a cluster. Per-device memory remains finite: frontier models and long contexts can still require model and state sharding Multi-GPU needed:

sections.text: "CPUs burn too much power per token" This is the final argument GPU advocates use. But the math changes dramatically when we look at realistic utilization , not theoretical peak FLOPS.

sections.text: GPU efficiency claims assume 100% compute utilization . Real inference doesn't work that way: Batch=1 latency: Most production inference is single-request Memory-bound: KV cache and weight loading dominate Token-to-token

sections.heading: What is SentencePiece?
sections.text: SentencePiece is a language-agnostic, unsupervised text tokenizer developed by Google (Kudo & Richardson, 2018). Unlike BPE which builds vocabulary bottom-up by merging frequent byte pairs, SentencePiece uses a unigram l

sections.heading: Globally Optimal
sections.text: Viterbi DP finds the token sequence that maximizes total score — unlike BPE's greedy merge-by-priority approach.

sections.heading: Byte Fallback
sections.text: Unknown characters decompose into byte tokens ( <0xE2> ), guaranteeing 100% coverage of any input.

sections.heading: Fully Reversible
sections.text: The ▁ (U+2581) space marker makes tokenization lossless — decode always reconstructs the original text exactly.

sections.heading: SentencePiece vs BPE vs WordPiece
sections.text: The three major tokenization algorithms take fundamentally different approaches to the same problem. Here's how they compare: Feature BPE (GPT-2) WordPiece (BERT) SentencePiece (LLaMA) Algorithm Merge by priority Greedy

sections.heading: The Unigram Language Model

sections.text: Finding the optimal tokenization naively would require checking all possible segmentations — exponential in text length. The Viterbi algorithm solves this in O(n × k) time using dynamic programming, where n is the text l

sections.heading: Space Handling: ▁ vs Ġ
sections.text: Space encoding is one of the most important — and most confusing — aspects of tokenization. SentencePiece and GPT-2 use incompatible strategies , and getting this wrong produces completely wrong tokenizations.

sections.heading: Tricky Cases & CK Behavior
sections.text: SentencePiece looks simple on paper, but there are a few subtle edge cases where implementations diverge. These are the ones that most often cause parity bugs. The CK tokenizer implements these behaviors explicitly so we

sections.heading: Leading and Trailing Spaces
sections.text: SentencePiece uses a dummy prefix ( ▁ ) for word starts. CK matches SPM’s whitespace normalization (collapse spaces, avoid double prefix), but only if the model’s config enables it. Some models disable the dummy prefix e

sections.heading: Unknown Runs
sections.text: When no token matches at a position, SPM inserts a single <unk> that can cover multiple consecutive bytes. CK tracks the unknown run length so one UNK covers the entire span, then merges consecutive UNKs to match Sentenc

sections.heading: Token Types Matter
sections.text: SPM vocab entries carry types (NORMAL, UNKNOWN, CONTROL, USER_DEFINED, UNUSED, BYTE). CK excludes CONTROL/UNUSED/BYTE from DP and gives USER_DEFINED tokens a score of 0 (as in llama.cpp), preventing rare but costly misma

sections.heading: Byte Fallback
sections.text: If no SPM tokenization exists, CK falls back to byte tokens using a fast 0-255 lookup table. This covers both raw byte tokens and <0xXX> style tokens when present. If a model lacks byte tokens, CK falls back to <unk> .

sections.heading: 1. Asset/Data Contract
sections.text: The asset library is the visual reference set and the context library is the semantic reference set. Source from docs/site/assets/*.svg or later public asset libraries. Strip literal text into placeholders first. Track l

sections.heading: 2. DSL Contract
sections.text: The DSL is the model boundary. It should describe composition and roles, not raw SVG bookkeeping. Emit scene choices such as layout, theme, rail, density, gap, background, and components. Use placeholders like heading_1

sections.heading: 3. Compiler Contract
sections.text: The compiler owns geometry, defs, gradients, markers, wrapping, and final render semantics. Compile scene DSL into SVG with deterministic layout rules. Guarantee round-trip reconstruction before any serious training run.

sections.heading: What We Are Actually Training
sections.text: In this line, the model is not being trained to be a free-form SVG artist. It is being trained to choose structured visual intent against a stable compiler contract.

sections.heading: Composition
sections.text: Composition means the overall information shape: compare two systems, show a pipeline, build a poster stack, or arrange dashboard cards. Examples: poster_stack , comparison_span_chart , pipeline_lane .

sections.heading: Layout Family
sections.text: Layout is the reusable geometry family inside the composition. It decides where headers, panels, tables, bars, and connectors belong. Examples: one tall poster, two compare panels, three-column dashboard, staged pipeline

sections.heading: Theme And Tone
sections.text: Theme is the visual language. Tone is the accent family inside that language. Examples: theme:infra_dark , theme:paper_editorial , tone:amber , tone:green .

sections.heading: Content Binding
sections.text: The content is not the same thing as the scene structure. The model should choose where content goes; a separate payload should provide what the text and values actually are. This is why later lines should move from lite

sections.heading: Worked Example
sections.text: A concrete keyed-scene example should look like this: Request prompt [task:svg] [layout:poster_stack] [topic:memory_reality] [theme:infra_dark] [tone:green] [density:compact] [OUT] Scene DSL emitted by the model [scene]

sections.heading: Topology Refs vs Content Refs
sections.text: Some richer layout families need more than content slots. Trees, maps, and graph-style layouts also need stable structural handles so the compiler knows what connects to what. Ref Type Example Used For Topology ref [node

sections.heading: Why Explicit Tokens Instead Of Generic BPE Right Now?
sections.text: Tokenizer architecture — the CK-Engine tokenizer uses explicit reserved tokens for the DSL surface. This makes every probe miss interpretable as a scene decision error, not subword spelling drift. The short answer is: be

sections.heading: Why not plain BPE first?
sections.text: If the tokenizer is free to break tags arbitrarily, a tiny model must learn both the scene language and the spelling of the scene language at the same time.

sections.heading: What explicit reserved tokens buy
sections.text: They make the contract visible. A probe miss can be read as the wrong scene decision instead of arbitrary subword drift across brackets, separators, and role markers.

sections.heading: Why this is not a universal rule
sections.text: Frontier models absolutely use learned tokenizers like BPE or SentencePiece at base-model scale. The explicit token surface here is a local engineering choice for a narrow formal DSL.

sections.heading: What should happen later
sections.text: Once the DSL is stable, revisit the tokenizer boundary as its own spec question: smaller reserved surface, learned merges, or mixed strategy. Do that after the contract is proven, not before. A useful rule is: Early line

sections.heading: Spec Lifecycle
sections.text: Evolution timeline — each spec passes through the same lifecycle stages below. The milestones above show how the v6.6 line matured through this exact process. 0

sections.heading: State the hypothesis
sections.text: Write down exactly what the next spec is trying to prove: richer DSL, better compiler, stronger asset family, or narrower repair. 1

sections.heading: Snapshot the assets
sections.text: Copy the chosen asset family into the cache-backed run workspace so the training contract is frozen and reproducible. 2

sections.heading: Replace literal text
sections.text: Strip shipped copy and replace it with placeholders. Train structure first, then bind content from a separate library. 3

sections.heading: Extract vocabulary
sections.text: Build the scene vocabulary from layouts, components, composition patterns, style families, and semantic text roles. 4

sections.heading: Prove the compiler
sections.text: Compile the DSL with dummy text and verify that the output is acceptably close to the reference asset family before training. 5

sections.heading: Freeze a gold asset gate
sections.text: Require a real gold pack, ideally 5 to 10 assets spanning comparison, poster, table, and pipeline families. Treat compiler fidelity as a gate, not a note. 6

sections.heading: Freeze the tokenizer surface
sections.text: Tokenize the DSL vocabulary plus placeholder text roles. Do not let arbitrary literal text dominate the tokenizer early, and do not keep whole component rows as permanent atomic tokens once the structure-content split is

sections.heading: Train with one primary axis
sections.text: Change one main thing per run: DSL, compiler, data mix, tokenizer budget, or capacity. Hold the rest stable. 8

sections.heading: Write the decision
sections.text: After every run, decide: promote, reject, repair, or branch. Every run ends with a next action, not just a score.

sections.heading: Operational Training Process
sections.text: The practical mistake is to let a rung answer too many questions at once. The better process is narrower: freeze measurement, name one failure class, teach family structure, and let validation close the last deterministi

sections.heading: Freeze measurement first
sections.text: Before changing the curriculum, freeze the probe prompt lists and keep them balanced across cases, forms, and prompt surfaces. Rule: if the probe contract changes, version it. Do not compare old and new runs as if they w

sections.heading: One rung, one question
sections.text: Every rung should target one named failure class: missing terminal tail, wrong family choice, wrong style bundle, stop-boundary spill, or broken exactness. Rule: if a rung changes grammar, probe shape, and repair mix tog

sections.heading: Train structure, not boilerplate
sections.text: The model should learn the family program: layout, components, refs, style controls, and counts. Deterministic tails and canonical ordering should be pushed into the compiler or repair layer whenever possible. Rule: do n

sections.heading: Add repair early
sections.text: Validation and repair are part of the system, not an admission of failure. Use them as soon as the family structure is mostly right and only a small deterministic residual remains. Rule: always report raw and repaired pr

sections.heading: Freeze the raw winner
sections.text: Keep the current raw champion as the comparison anchor. New runs compete against that run, not against train loss or operator intuition. Rule: promotion gates should reference one frozen probe report and one frozen best

sections.heading: Pilot before full rung
sections.text: If a repair idea touches shared-family behavior, run a small pilot first. Scale the token budget down and treat the result as a gate, not an automatic successor rung. Rule: a full rung stays blocked until the pilot impro

sections.heading: Decode first after strong raw runs
sections.text: Once the raw line is mostly correct, push stop-boundary, prompt-spill, and deterministic cleanup into decode, validation, and repair before spending another broad training cycle. Rule: if the miss set is mostly repairabl

sections.heading: Ban literal prompt junk repair rows
sections.text: Do not teach the model the exact wrapper junk you want it to avoid. That turns the warning language itself into the target distribution. Rule: use control-agnostic clean-stop prompts rather than rows that spell out [OUT]

sections.heading: Context Budget Is A Gate
sections.text: Do not guess the next context length. Measure the gold scenes with the current tokenizer family before training. Rule Interpretation p95(prompt + output) < 400 ctx=512 is probably still enough. 400-600 Move to ctx=768 on

sections.heading: How To Build Frontier-Style Intuition
sections.text: No serious engineer would laugh at the core idea here. The separation of structure, content, compiler, and eval is exactly the kind of thinking that makes systems reliable. What strong teams would challenge is not the di

sections.heading: Good instinct
sections.text: Separating asset library, scene DSL, content, compiler, and probe contracts is a strong instinct. It reduces ambiguity and makes failures legible.

sections.heading: What frontier teams would push harder on
sections.text: Cleaner ablations, stricter gates, more automatic validation, less manual drift between specs, and fewer simultaneous changes per run.

sections.heading: What to copy from them
sections.text: Treat every run like an experiment with a written hypothesis, a fixed baseline, a canary, a non-regression gate, and a clear promotion or rejection rule.

sections.text: Spec19 Textbook Routing Mixture spec19 is the recommended next branch after the bounded-intent experiments on top of the frozen spec16 scene-bundle winner. The point is not to keep churning near-identical routing rungs.

sections.heading: Spec17 Fixed The Question
sections.text: spec17 established the real problem: bounded intent is a planning task, not just a syntax task. It also forced better audits and cleaner contrast coverage.

sections.heading: Spec18 Fixed The Launch Shape
sections.text: spec18 kept the same compiler, renderer, tokenizer, and shared [bundle] contract while testing a routing-first curriculum. The run path was correct and reproducible.

sections.heading: Held-Out Routing Still Failed
sections.text: spec18 r1 ended with overall exactness around 4.8% , but visible and hidden held-out exactness stayed at 0% . That means the remaining problem is not a missing guardrail. It is still a data and capacity question.

sections.heading: What To Copy From The Papers And The NVIDIA Dataset Lesson
Named Mixtures, Not One Blob
sections.text: The useful lesson from NVIDIA's large public pretraining collections is organizational: split the corpus into named components with explicit provenance and mixture control. For CK-native training, that means versioned bu

sections.heading: phi-1: Increase Structural Density
sections.text: Prefer clean, compiler-validated, textbook-style teaching rows over more noisy coverage. The next branch should spend more mass on direct routing supervision and minimal pairs than on broad scaffold language.

sections.heading: Grokking: Stop Same-Shape Churn
sections.text: If loss moves and held-out exactness stays flat, that is a block on repeating the same training style. Another spec18 rung with the same recipe would likely add cost without adding clarity.

sections.heading: HumanEval / Codex: Measure Correctness
sections.text: Renderable-but-wrong rows are semantic failures, not wins. Promotion should still depend on held-out exactness. Sidecar best-of- k analysis can help diagnose whether the model knows more than greedy decode shows.

sections.heading: CodeT5: Score Fields, Not Just Strings
sections.text: Bundle tags behave like code identifiers with constrained semantics. That means evaluation should separate syntax from family, form, style, and topology errors instead of collapsing everything into one exact-match bucket

sections.heading: AlphaCode: Generate Then Filter
sections.text: The compiler is a structural oracle. Best-of- k decode plus compiler filtering is a valid sidecar metric and practical inference path when syntax is close but greedy decode is brittle.

sections.heading: Nemotron: Curate The Mixture Explicitly
sections.text: The dataset lesson is operational, not mystical: keep named buckets, provenance, dedupe discipline, and measured mix ratios. The run artifact directory should record those manifests so the branch can be replayed or shipp

sections.heading: Keep Fixed
sections.text: Seed from frozen spec16 r9 . Freeze the tokenizer unless a tokenizer branch is the explicit axis. Keep the same shared [bundle] ... [/bundle] output contract. Keep the same deterministic renderer and compiler boundary.

sections.heading: Change One Main Thing
sections.text: Change the dataset philosophy, not the whole stack at once. Move to named mixture buckets. Increase direct routebook density and minimal-pair coverage. Separate any later capacity step into its own branch decision.

sections.heading: Do Not Regress Into
sections.text: warning-language repair rows raw SVG targets prompt-contamination teaching blurry runs that change curriculum and capacity together

sections.text: Bucket Purpose Typical contents Anchor Replay Preserve closure and exact bundle syntax. Explicit bundle anchors, clean-stop anchors, permuted explicit anchors. Routebook Direct Teach topic + goal + audience -> family + f

sections.heading: Spec19 R1 Canary
sections.text: Keep the current architecture first. The question is whether the routebook mixture changes held-out exactness without introducing new stack risk. same frozen tokenizer same spec16 r9 seed same shared bundle contract full

sections.heading: Gate For Promotion
sections.text: Require nonzero exactness on both visible held-out splits and at least one hidden split. Renderability alone is not enough.

sections.heading: If It Is Still Zero
sections.text: Treat that as a clean signal that the current model size may be the limit. Run a separate capacity canary on the same spec19 dataset recipe instead of silently changing data and model size together.

sections.text: Operator Spectrum The full pipeline from raw data to inference — a continuous refinement loop. Click any stage to see what it does, which docs pages cover it, and what to tune next. 1 📦 Data Raw corpus SVG, text, JSON →

sections.heading: 📦 Stage 1 — Data
sections.text: Everything starts here. The quality and structure of your raw corpus determines the ceiling for everything downstream. For SVG training: validate ASCII-only, deduplicate near-identical rows, add explicit <eos> boundaries

sections.heading: 🔤 Stage 2 — Tokenizer
sections.text: Converts raw text into integer token sequences the model can process. BPE learns merge rules from the corpus; vocab size directly affects model capacity. The encode→decode roundtrip must be lossless — any artifact here p

sections.heading: ⚙️ Stage 3 — Data Preparation
sections.text: Token sequences are chunked into fixed-length windows, batched, and optionally shuffled. Sequence length determines how much context the model sees per step; batch size × grad accumulation steps = effective batch. A trai

sections.heading: 🧠 Stage 4 — AI Algorithm (Model Architecture)
sections.text: The Transformer architecture — attention heads, feed-forward layers, embeddings. The IR defines the computational graph; codegen compiles it to C kernels. This is where you choose how many layers, heads, embed dimensions

sections.heading: ▶️ Stage 5 — Forward Pass
sections.text: Input tokens flow through embedding → attention → FFN → output logits. Each kernel (matmul, softmax, layernorm, RoPE) runs as optimized C with SIMD intrinsics. Memory layout (row-major vs. transposed) and tiling strategy

sections.heading: ◀️ Stage 6 — Backward Pass
sections.text: Gradients flow backward through the chain rule. Each forward kernel has a corresponding backward kernel that computes dL/dW and dL/dx . Gradient accumulation lets you simulate larger batches on limited memory. Watch for

sections.heading: 📉 Stage 7 — Loss & Evaluation
sections.text: Cross-entropy loss measures how far the model's predictions are from ground truth. Decreasing loss ≠ good model; you need eval metrics: valid SVG rate, exact-match rate, prompt-to-SVG success. Compare train loss vs. val

sections.heading: ✨ Stage 8 — Inference
sections.text: The payoff. Feed a prompt, generate tokens auto-regressively until </svg> or <eos> . Temperature and top-k control creativity vs. coherence. If the output loops or generates artifacts, the fix is usually upstream: better

sections.heading: Case Study: Finding the RoPE Bug
sections.text: This methodology found a subtle RoPE rotation convention bug that caused predictions to diverge at later context positions.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: - Kernel tests: PASSED (1e-5 precision) - Layer tests: PASSED (1e-5 precision) - Full forward: FAILED (predictions diverge at position 3+)

sections.heading: Investigation
sections.text: 1. Kernel tests passed → kernels are correct for SOME convention 2. Layer tests passed → same story 3. But full model failed → bug is in convention, not math 4. Per-stage diff showed: q/k looked "correct" but were wrong

sections.heading: Root Cause
sections.text: Our RoPE: (x[0], x[1]), (x[2], x[3]), ... (interleaved pairs) Llama/SmolLM: (x[0..half], x[half..dim]) (rotate-half) Both are mathematically valid RoPE, but weights are trained for one convention.

sections.heading: Fix
sections.text: 1. Update C kernel: src/kernels/rope_kernels.c 2. Update Python references: unittest/test_rope.py, scripts/smollm_layer_stage_diff.py 3. Re-run all tests: ALL PASS

sections.text: Lifecycle: Create → Dispatch → Destroy

sections.heading: 1. Create —
sections.text: ck_threadpool_create(n_threads) Called once at engine startup. Allocates the pool struct (cache-line aligned), then spawns N−1 worker pthreads. Workers immediately enter the spin-wait loop. The main thread is thread 0 —

sections.heading: 2. Dispatch (called ~500x per token) —
sections.text: ck_threadpool_dispatch(pool, fn, args) Sets the work function + args, bumps n_dispatch (an atomic counter), and signals sleeping workers via condvar. Main thread also runs its share. All threads do their chunk, then main

sections.heading: 3. Pause/Resume (between batches)
sections.text: Between user interactions (waiting for input), workers can be paused so they sleep on a condvar and use 0% CPU. Resume wakes them instantly.

sections.heading: 4. Destroy —
sections.text: ck_threadpool_destroy(pool) Sets stop = 1 , broadcasts the condvar to wake sleeping workers, then pthread_join s every worker thread. Frees the pool memory.

sections.text: Spin-Wait vs. Sleep: The Hybrid Polling Design How do worker threads wait for work? There are two extremes, and CK-Engine uses both.

sections.heading: Pure Spin-Wait
sections.text: Thread sits in a tight loop checking an atomic variable: while (no_work) { _mm_pause(); } PRO: Instant wake-up (nanoseconds) CON: Burns 100% CPU while waiting

sections.heading: Pure Condvar Sleep

sections.text: _mm_pause() ? It's an x86 intrinsic that tells the CPU: "I'm in a spin-wait loop." The CPU can then: Reduce power consumption of the spinning core Free up execution resources for the sibling hyper-thread Avoid memory-ord

sections.heading: §7
sections.text: Atomics, Mutexes, and Memory Ordering These are the fundamental building blocks of any concurrent system. Let's understand each one from scratch.

sections.heading: What Is an Atomic Operation?
sections.text: An atomic operation is one that completes in a single, indivisible step from the perspective of all other threads. No other thread can see a "half-done" state. WITHOUT atomics (broken): WITH atomics (correct): Thread A:

sections.heading: Memory Ordering
sections.text: CPUs and compilers can reorder memory operations for performance. Memory ordering tells them: "don't reorder this particular operation past certain points." Ordering What It Means Used In CK-Engine For memory_order_relax

sections.heading: What Is a Mutex?
sections.text: A mutex (mutual exclusion) is a lock. Only one thread can hold it at a time. Everyone else waits. CK-Engine uses mutexes only for the condvar sleep mechanism — the hot path (spin-wait) doesn't touch the mutex at all. //

sections.heading: What Is a Condition Variable (Condvar)?
sections.text: A condvar lets a thread say: "Wake me up when something changes." It works together with a mutex: Wait side: Lock mutex → check condition → if false, cond_wait (atomically releases mutex + sleeps) → on wake, re-acquires

sections.heading: §8
sections.text: Cache Lines & False Sharing This is one of the most important performance concepts in multi-threaded code.

sections.heading: How CPU Caches Work (Simplified)
sections.text: CPUs don't read individual bytes from RAM. They read in cache lines — 64-byte chunks. When one core writes to a cache line, all other cores that have a copy of that line must invalidate it (MESI protocol). This is called

sections.heading: §9
sections.text: The Barrier: How Threads Synchronize A barrier is a meeting point. All threads must arrive before any can proceed. CK-Engine implements a custom spin-wait barrier using two atomic counters: n_arrived (how many threads re

sections.heading: §11
sections.text: Thread Pool vs. Memory Pool — Same Idea, Different Resource Both are "pools" — they pre-create expensive resources. The key differences are about what they pool and what synchronization they need. Aspect Thread Pool Memo

sections.heading: The Deeper Conceptual Link
sections.text: The pool pattern in both cases: Thread Pool Memory Pool +---------------------+ +---------------------+ | STARTUP (once) | | STARTUP (once) | | Create N threads | | malloc(big_block) | | All threads idle | | Carve into s

sections.heading: Thread Pool Sync
sections.text: atomic_int for dispatch/complete counters (hot path). pthread_mutex + cond for sleep fallback (cold path). _mm_pause() spin hint for low-latency wake. memory_order_acquire/release to publish work descriptor.

sections.heading: Memory Pool Sync
sections.text: Atomic CAS for lock-free free-list (typical). Or a simple mutex around the free-list pointer. Bump allocator variant needs zero sync (per-thread pools). No condvars needed — memory doesn't need to "wake up."

sections.heading: §12
sections.text: Why Is It Faster?

sections.heading: Cost Breakdown: OpenMP vs. Thread Pool
sections.text: Per-kernel dispatch cost comparison (4 threads, x86-64): OpenMP fork/join: +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | pthread_create x3 | work | pthread_join x3 | scheduler | | ~~~100 us~~~~~~

sections.heading: 1. No Thread Creation
sections.text: pthread_create involves a system call, stack allocation (~8MB virtual), kernel scheduling setup, and TLS initialization. The thread pool does this once . Subsequent dispatches just flip an atomic counter — a single CPU i

sections.heading: 2. No Join Overhead
sections.text: pthread_join involves a system call + scheduler interaction to reap the thread. The pool never joins during work — completion is tracked with a simple atomic counter.

sections.text: 100% HuggingFace Parity C-Kernel BPE Tokenizer From raw bytes to token IDs — one beautiful merge at a time. A visual, Feynman-style walkthrough of Byte Pair Encoding.

sections.heading: The One-Sentence Idea
sections.text: Find the most common pair of adjacent symbols, replace every occurrence with a single new symbol, and repeat. That's the entire algorithm.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: BPE on Our SVG Dataset
sections.text: Our BPE trainer ( ck-bpe-train ) feeds on .svg , .txt , .html , .md , and .json files from the corpus. Let's trace the algorithm on a tiny SVG fragment: <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24"> <path d="M12 2L2 22h20z"/> </svg>

sections.heading: Step 1 — Split Into Bytes
sections.text: Every byte of every file in the corpus becomes a base symbol . IDs 0–3 are reserved for special tokens; IDs 4–259 cover all 256 byte values.

sections.heading: Step 2 — Count Every Adjacent Pair
sections.text: Scan the entire corpus (multi-threaded, one shard per file). For every position i , record the pair (seq[i], seq[i+1]) in a hash table. Why does this matter for SVGs? SVG files repeat patterns like <path d=" , stroke=" ,

sections.heading: Step 3 — Pick the Top Pair & Merge It
sections.text: The pair with the highest count wins (ties broken by smallest ID pair for determinism). It gets assigned the next available token ID, and every occurrence in the corpus is replaced in one pass.

sections.heading: Step 4 — Repeat Until vocab_size
sections.text: Each iteration: count → pick → merge → shrink. Pairs can now include previously merged tokens , so the algorithm builds longer and longer pieces.

sections.text: Per micro-step CE with mean reduction gives: \[ \nabla z = \frac{p - \text{one\_hot}}{N} \] After accumulating K micro-steps, the optimizer must consume the average gradient: \[ g_{\text{step}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{m=1}^{K

sections.heading: Why This Mattered at lr = 1e-3
sections.text: If accumulated gradients are not divided by K , optimizer input is approximately K times too large. K=8 with lr=1e-3 behaves closer to an effective step size like ~8e-3 in magnitude. This can look fine early, then destab

sections.heading: Variable Context Length Caveat (Important on CPU)
sections.text: When sequence lengths vary per micro-step, N can vary too. That means naive fixed scaling can bias updates.

sections.heading: Robust Strategy for Variable-Length Windows
sections.text: Track valid-token counts per micro-step (post-ignore filtering). Accumulate gradients in numerator form or keep per-step weighted scaling. Normalize by total valid targets in the full accumulation window, not a fixed con

sections.heading: Operator Checklist
sections.text: Set grad_accum from memory budget and desired effective batch. Confirm one optimizer update per full window. Confirm accumulated gradient averaging ( /K ) before AdamW. Use long-horizon parity checks with fixed token str

sections.heading: Bottom Line
sections.text: CE math correctness ( p - one_hot , /N ) is necessary but not sufficient. Production-stable backprop also requires window-correct optimizer scaling ( /K ) so CPU batch simulation behaves like true larger-batch training.

sections.heading: Before

sections.heading: Failure Mode
sections.text: Two mathematically different kernels looked interchangeable because both were called “attention.” Unit tests exercised a correct leaf while generated code reached another route.

sections.heading: After
